analysis.one_liner: Requires banks to get written consent before charging overdraft fees and stops reordering transactions to trigger them.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the House Financial Services Committee for the rest of the 110th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: Banks and credit unions routinely enroll customers in overdraft coverage without asking and then charge fees — often around $30 each — when an account runs short. This bill would have required written consent before any overdraft fee could be charged, given consumers a real-time notice at ATMs and debit terminals before a fee was incurred, shown only actual account balances at ATMs, banned misleading ads like calling a fee-charging account 'free', and prohibited banks from processing transactions out of order to maximize fees. It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and died there without a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Checking account customers, especially low-income households who overdraft most often — they'd keep hundreds of dollars a year in fees and see balances reflect actual money available rather than including phantom overdraft credit.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Checking account customers who get hit with overdraft fees

how_it_helps.text: Requires specific written consent before a bank can charge overdraft fees, ending automatic enrollment in fee-triggering overdraft programs [S3].
Bans banks from delaying deposits or reordering check and debit postings in ways that manufacture overdraft fees [S3].

Requires ATMs and debit terminals to warn the consumer before completing a transaction that will trigger a fee, and requires ATM balance inquiries to show the true balance rather than including phantom overdraft credit [S3].
Prohibits advertising an overdraft-fee account as 'free' or as a way to meet short-term credit needs, and bans claims a bank will honor all checks when it retains discretion not to [S3].
Limits fee-free incidental overdraft coverage to three fees per calendar year absent a signed agreement [S3].
Requires overdraft fees to be counted in the account's disclosed annual percentage rate and shown separately on each periodic statement [S3].
Clarifies that banks cannot dodge the rules by simply charging the same fee for a returned (bounced) item [S3].
Requires institutions to disclose when they will not pay an overdraft, and bans misrepresenting discretionary coverage as a guarantee [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Banks, credit unions, and other depository institutions that collect overdraft fee revenue; fintech-like bank programs marketing overdraft as short-term credit would also face advertising restrictions. Compliance costs are modest.
analysis.who_pays_short: Banks and credit unions that charge overdraft fees

drawbacks.text: Some consumers who would affirmatively opt in could still face high fees, and banks might respond by raising other fees, closing low-balance accounts, or dropping courtesy coverage — a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge [S3].
The consent, notice, and disclosure requirements would add compliance costs for smaller banks and credit unions [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer benefit is clear and direct: fewer surprise fees and honest balances at the ATM. The costs fall on banks' fee revenue and add modest compliance burden; the ban on transaction reordering targets a practice that is hard to defend in good faith. The bill is limited to overdraft fees rather than banning them outright, which preserves genuine opt-in coverage.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced and then to a subcommittee in April 2007; no markup, vote, or further action ever occurred before the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Introduced February 8, 2007 by Rep. Carolyn Maloney with Reps. Barney Frank and Julia Carson as original cosponsors and 31 total cosponsors (30 Democrats, 1 Republican) [S1, S4].
Referred to the House Committee on Financial Services on February 8, 2007 [S1].
Referred to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit on April 12, 2007, where it remained [S1, S5].
No committee report, markup, floor vote, or further action is recorded through the end of the 110th Congress on January 3, 2009 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks and credit unions that collect overdraft fee revenue — estimated in the tens of billions of dollars annually — avoided new restrictions on automatic enrollment, ATM warnings, balance disclosures, and transaction reordering. Consumers continued paying the fees.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Banks and credit unions collecting overdraft fees

for.name: Rep. Carolyn Maloney
for.role: Sponsor; House Financial Services Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its precursor versions and pressed for overdraft fee restrictions in committee.

for.name: Rep. Barney Frank
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor; as committee chair, never brought the bill to a markup or vote.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee and held no markup or vote for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: Banking industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed restrictions on overdraft fee practices during this period; Congress ultimately left regulation to the Federal Reserve, whose 2010 rule required only opt-in rather than the fuller protections in this bill.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was overwhelmingly Democratic (30 of 31), suggesting the issue broke along party lines, but the bill never reached a vote so no roll-call record exists.

industries.note: They collect large overdraft fee revenue — often from customers who can least afford it — and this bill would cut directly into it by requiring written consent, real-time warnings, true balance displays, honest advertising, and a ban on reordering transactions to trigger fees. Consumers bore the cost of those fees.

industries.industry: Fintech and marketing of overdraft as short-term credit
industries.note: Banks advertising overdraft coverage as a substitute for payday-style short-term loans would be barred from those claims.
